title: Intersections & Turns
summary: How to approach intersections, set up and finish right and left turns, use turn lanes and roundabouts, and turn around safely.

items: Stop behind the stop line. If there is no line, stop before the crosswalk. If there is neither, stop before the intersection where you can see cross traffic.
If parked vehicles block your view after stopping, creep forward slowly until you can see.
Look left, then right, then left again before you pull out. Traffic from the left is closest to you, so check it twice.
Check the crosswalks for people about to cross, not just for cars.
Even on a green light, do not enter until there is room on the far side for your whole car.
In slow traffic, stop before a side street entrance so you leave it open for others.
A turn signal tells others what you plan to do. Turn it on before you slow down and turn, so they have time to react.
How many feet before a turn you must signal is set by state law; check your State Cheat Sheet.
Move into the correct lane well ahead of the turn.
Turn from the lane closest to the direction you are going unless signs or markings allow other lanes.
After the turn, make sure your signal has turned off.
Look through the turn, toward where you want to go.

blocks.text: If your signals fail, use hand signals with your left arm: straight out for a left turn, bent up for a right turn, bent down to slow or stop.

items: Signal and move close to the right curb or edge of the road well before the corner.
Check your right mirror and right blind spot for bicyclists, motorcyclists and pedestrians.
Slow down and yield to pedestrians crossing the street you are turning onto.
Turn into the lane closest to the right curb. If you need another lane later, finish the turn first and then change lanes safely.

blocks.text: Do not swing left before a right turn. It leaves room on your right for a car or bike to slip in, and it confuses drivers behind you.

From a one-way street, turn right from the far-right lane unless signs or markings say otherwise. Remember that your rear wheels follow a shorter path than your front wheels and cut closer to the curb, so do not cut the corner.

rows: Start just to the right of the center line.
Two lanes on the new street
End in the lane closest to the center line, so you do not conflict with oncoming drivers turning right.
Wide median on a divided highway
Cross the near roadway, then turn left into the far roadway.

items: When you and an oncoming driver both turn left, each of you turns before reaching the center of the intersection.
While you wait, keep your front wheels pointed straight. If you are hit from behind, you will not be pushed into oncoming traffic.
If an oncoming car has its right signal on, wait until it actually starts to turn before you go.
If a driver in the near lane waves you on, make sure the far lane is clear before you turn.
A protected left turn is one where a signal, such as a green arrow, stops oncoming traffic while you turn.

blocks.text: To use a center two-way left-turn lane, check for oncoming drivers already in it, signal, and move fully into the lane shortly before your turn. It is not a travel lane, and drivers from the other direction use it too.

items: With two side-by-side turn lanes, stay in your own lane from start to finish and end in the matching lane. From the right-hand of two left-turn lanes, end in the second lane from the center line.
Watch for the vehicle beside you drifting into your lane during a double turn.
If you are in a turn-only lane but wanted to go straight, make the turn the lane requires, then find another route.
If heavy traffic keeps you from reaching your turn lane, skip this turn and take the next safe route.
If you start turning onto the wrong street, finish the turn, then find a safe place to turn around.

blocks.text: A truck's or bus's rear wheels cut well inside its front wheels, so large vehicles often swing wide to turn.

items: If a truck signals right but moves left first, it is making room for its turn. Stay behind it; never pull into the space on its right.
When stopped at a light, stay behind the stop line so a turning truck has room to swing into your street.

blocks.caption: Travel counterclockwise, to the right of the center island

items: Slow down and watch for pedestrians in the crosswalk.

Pick your lane before you enter, using the signs, pavement arrows and your exit. In a two-lane roundabout, use the right lane to turn right and the left lane to turn left or make a U-turn, unless signs show otherwise. Going straight, follow the lane arrows.
Yield to traffic already in the roundabout, then enter to the right and travel counterclockwise to your exit, even if it is on the left.
Inside, keep moving and do not change lanes. Stop only to avoid a crash.
Use your right turn signal as you approach your exit, and yield to pedestrians in the exit crosswalk.
If you miss your exit, keep going around until you come back to it. Never back up in a roundabout.
Do not drive beside a large truck in a roundabout; give it room.
The raised paved area by the central island, called a truck apron, is for the rear wheels of large trucks, not for cars.
Stay behind a bicyclist riding in the lane of a single-lane roundabout.
When waiting in line to enter, stop behind the crosswalk to keep it clear.
Never make a U-turn where a NO U-TURN sign is posted, even if no one is coming.
U-turns are most dangerous near the top of a hill or on a curve, where others cannot see you. Go on to a place with a clear view.
On a divided highway, U-turn only at a median opening where it is not prohibited.
On a busy highway, the safest way to turn around is to use a side road or lot and re-enter going forward.
A three-point turn is for a narrow, quiet street where a U-turn will not fit.
Other U-turn rules, such as in business districts, vary by state; check your State Cheat Sheet.

keyPoints: Stop behind the stop line or crosswalk, then look left, right and left again.
Signal before you slow down, and get into the correct lane well ahead of the turn.
Right turns: hug the right curb and end in the right lane. Left turns: start near the center line and end in the lane closest to it.
Keep your wheels straight while waiting to turn left.
Never enter an intersection unless you can get all the way across.
Give large trucks room; their rear wheels cut inside the turn.
In a roundabout, yield to traffic inside, go counterclockwise, and signal right to exit.
No U-turns where posted, on hills or curves, or where others cannot see you.
